analysis.one_liner: Orders regulators to impose position limits and margin rules on oil and fuel speculation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required federal caps on speculative trading in oil and gasoline markets, was referred to a Senate committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2011, gas prices were high and the bill's sponsors argued that Wall Street speculators—not supply and demand—were pushing them up. The bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, within two weeks of passage, to cap how much speculators could bet in crude oil, gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and heating oil markets, and to require 12% margin (down payment) on speculative trades. It exempted legitimate hedging by actual oil producers and buyers. The bill was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee and died there without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses that buy gasoline, diesel, heating oil, and jet fuel would benefit if limiting speculation lowers fuel prices, as the bill's findings argue it would. Airlines, truckers, and other fuel-heavy businesses would also gain from lower and less volatile fuel costs.

how_it_helps.text: Within 14 days of enactment, the CFTC Chairman would have to impose speculative position limits on crude oil, gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and heating oil futures and swaps, matching the limits the New York Mercantile Exchange had set.
The bill would require a 12% margin requirement on speculative energy futures and swaps, raising the cash speculators must post and discouraging leveraged bets.

Banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and swaps dealers trading energy futures for themselves or for index funds and ETFs would have to register as speculators and face the same limits, closing routes around the caps.
Bona-fide hedge trading by real producers, refiners, and end users of fuel would remain exempt, so legitimate risk management would not be restricted.
The bill stated its purpose was to make fuel prices reflect supply and demand fundamentals, citing evidence it presented that speculation had added tens of dollars to the per-barrel price of oil.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, hedge funds, and other financial firms that profit from large speculative positions in energy markets would bear the cost of reduced trading profits and higher margin requirements. If limiting speculation reduced trading revenue at exchanges, they would share that cost.

drawbacks.text: Economists disagree about how much speculation affects oil prices; if the bill's premise overstated speculation's role, the caps would do little to lower gas prices while constraining trading.

The bill would have ordered the CFTC Chairman to act unilaterally within 14 days, bypassing normal rulemaking procedures and the Commission's vote, an approach critics could call an overreach that invites legal challenge.
Position limits set at levels matching one exchange (NYMEX) could push speculative trading to foreign or unregulated venues, shifting activity rather than eliminating it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill's diagnosis was right—that speculators were adding tens of dollars per barrel—the benefit to consumers and fuel-reliant businesses would be substantial and the cost limited to speculative trading profits. The main risk is that the caps might not lower prices much if fundamentals, not speculation, drove the 2011 spike. The speed and mechanism ( unilateral 14-day directive) was aggressive but responsive to the fact that the CFTC had already missed its Dodd-Frank deadline. The strongest cost is that reduced speculation can thin market liquidity, potentially making prices more volatile in the short run.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on June 15, 2011, citing findings that gas at $3.75 a gallon exceeded what supply and demand fundamentals justified and that CFTC had not yet imposed the position limits Dodd-Frank required.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which had jurisdiction over commodities trading.
No further action was ever recorded—no hearings, no markup, no vote—through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, hedge funds, and other financial firms trading oil and fuel futures are better off, since the speculative position limits and 12% margin requirements were never imposed. The CFTC also avoided the 14-day unilateral mandate. (In the real world, the CFTC's own position-limit rule was later vacated by a court in 2012, and limits were not reinstated until years later, so speculative trading in energy markets continued unimpeded during this period.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy speculators and big trading banks

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks arguing that speculators were driving up gas prices and that the CFTC was required by Dodd-Frank to act.

for.name: Bill Nelson, Richard Blumenthal, Jeff Merkley, Al Franken, Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senators (D) who joined Sanders in introducing the bill
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsors who put their names on the bill at introduction.

for.name: 3 additional Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors who signed on after introduction
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to the sponsor plus 8 cosponsors, all Democratic.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over commodities markets
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never held a markup, hearing on the bill, or vote, so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill sat, never scheduled it for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All of the bill's support came from Democratic and Independent senators—Sanders plus 8 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican support recorded—while the Democratic-controlled committee allowed it to die.

industries.industry: Energy speculators (banks, hedge funds, index funds and ETFs trading oil futures and swaps)
industries.note: The bill would have capped their positions, required registration as speculators, and imposed 12% margin, directly cutting into profits from leveraged energy bets. If the bill's premise held, those profits came at the expense of higher prices for everyone who buys fuel.

Speculative volume would be capped and margin raised, reducing trading revenue, though the bill used the exchange's own accountability levels as the limit, limiting disruption to its market structure.

Airlines testified that oil's marginal cost was $60-70 a barrel, well below the market price; limiting speculation promised lower fuel costs. Delta's general counsel was quoted in the bill's findings.

industries.industry: Oil producers and commercial fuel users (bona-fide hedgers)
industries.note: They are explicitly exempted from position limits and margin requirements, so legitimate hedging would keep its privileged status in the market.
